findings.title: Key guard no longer rejects undefined/falsy keys
findings.claim: The guard was narrowed from a falsy test (`!key`) to `key === null || key.length === 0` (src/idem.ts:2). The two forms are equivalent only for the declared `string | null` domain. For `undefined` — the ordinary runtime representation of an absent key — the first operand is false and `key.length` is evaluated on undefined, so the function now throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` instead of its intended `Error('missing idempotency key')`. Other falsy, non-null values (0, false, NaN) do not match either operand and the call returns 1, i.e. a missing/invalid idempotency key is accepted, whereas the old guard rejected them. Until this change, any caller on the JS boundary, or one compiled without strictNullChecks (where `run(undefined)`/`run(null)` are type-legal), received the deliberate rejection; now it gets an uncontrolled TypeError or no error at all. The declared type hides this regression only from strictly-typed callers.

findings.title: Narrowed key guard drops falsy non-string inputs; undefined now throws TypeError
findings.claim: The changed guard `if (key === null || key.length === 0)` only rejects `null` and zero-length strings, so it is no longer equivalent to the previous falsy check for runtime inputs outside the declared `string | null` type. Calling the exported `run` with `undefined` (e.g. a JS caller, a missing argument, or a TS caller compiled without strictNullChecks) evaluates `key === null` as false and then reads `key.length`, throwing an unhandled `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` instead of the intended `Error('missing idempotency key')` that the base guard produced. Other falsy non-strings such as `0`, `false` and `NaN` make both comparisons false, so the guard falls through and `run` returns 1 — a missing/invalid idempotency key is silently accepted, regressing the validation fixed at the merge-base and contradicting the API contract that `run` rejects null or empty idempotency keys.
findings.trigger: Invoke `run(undefined)` / `run()` (no argument) from JavaScript or a non-strict-null-checked TypeScript caller, or `run(0 as any)` / `run(false as any)` (e.g. a key sourced from unvalidated JSON/config); the first case crashes with TypeError before the validation error is raised, the latter cases return 1 without rejecting the key.

evidence.description: The only changed line: the falsy guard `!key` was replaced by `key === null || key.length === 0`, narrowing which invalid inputs are rejected.

Head implementation: after `key === null` is false, `key.length` is dereferenced for every other input; a non-null falsy non-string has no numeric length (or throws for undefined) so the missing/empty-key error is not raised.

Merge-base implementation (`if (!key) throw ...`, commit 6302efff) rejected all falsy values, including undefined, 0, false and NaN; the new guard no longer covers them, proving the regression is introduced by this diff.

Documented contract: `run rejects null or empty idempotency keys before returning.` The changed guard no longer enforces this for any non-null, non-string falsy key value, and crashes rather than rejecting when the key is undefined.
